title: Spin-transition modulated light-emitting devices in a 2D magnet

paper_content.abstract:
Emerging two-dimensional magnetic semiconductors represent transformative platforms to
explore magneto-optics and opto-spintronic applications. Though two-dimensional opto-
spintronics has attracted tremendous research efforts in spin-dependent photodetectors and non-
volatile memory components, the realization of one core application - spin-modulated light-
emitting device - remains elusive so far. Here we successfully realize prototype spin-modulated
light-emitting device integrated with a two-dimensional semiconducting magnet chromium sulfide
bromide, demonstrating considerable electroluminescence down to bilayers. Intriguingly, its
discovered to be directly manipulated by spin-flip and spin-canting transitions. Notably, the
intrinsic carrier-tunable interlayer magnetic coupling in chromium sulfide bromide enables
electroluminescence to actively amplify magnetic hysteresis (via spin-flip) and continuously tune
magnetic order (via spin-canting) with robust anisotropy, establishing a connection between carrier
injection, magnetic phase transitions, and optical emission. The prototype demonstration of spin-
modulated light-emitting device establishes an indispensable scheme of opto-spintronic devices
leveraging two-dimensional spin transitions and strong excitonic effects, presenting a critical step
towards integrated two-dimensional opto-spintronics.
paper_content.introduction:
Opto-spintronics, merging photonic, electronic, and magnetic functionalities, becomes a
novel but desirable paradigm for future information technologies1-4. Compared with conventional
charge-based electronics, this paradigm exploits electron spins as the fundamental variable for
information processing and storage, promising new functionalities with significantly reduced
energy consumption. For instance, non-volatile memory devices feature optical writing and
electrical readout of the spin orders5,6, and neuromorphic computing hardware employ spin-based
artificial synapses7. By leveraging spin-wave excitations, opto-magnonic circuits and quantum
transduction platforms have also been proposed and developed8. As one of the fundamental
optoelectronic components, light-emitting devices (LEDs) advance to unexplored versatility when
their electrical injections involve profound spin manipulations9-12. A critical bottleneck in opto-
spintronics is cryogenic operation (<10 K) of spin-dependent effects, far from practical room-
temperature requirements. This stems from the thermal fragility of two-dimensional (2D) magnetic
order and enhanced non-radiative recombination in 2D semiconductors.

The emerging vdW magnets have been recently extensively studied for striking fundamental
physical breakthroughs with unconventional 2D magnetism13,14. The confluence of inherent 2D
magnetism, electronic structures, and weak dielectric screening in the layered structures suggests
unprecedented functionalities to opto-spintronic components9. For example, spin-dependent
photodetectors15-17, spin-photovoltaics18 with magnetic CrI and MnSe have been proposed;
3
Moreover, non-volatile memory component with magnetic four-layer CrI and VSe has also been
3 2
designed19. However, as one core application of 2D opto-spintronics, no LED with spin-based
functionality has been realized so far20-23. Here, we report the realization of a prototype spin-
modulated LED (spin-LED) in CrSBr-based quantum well (QW) structures, achieving
considerable electroluminescence (EL) down to bilayer CrSBr. Unlike EL in conventional
semiconductors dictated by band structure and carrier recombinations24-27, the spin-exciton
coupling in CrSBr introduces versatile manipulations of its EL. Remarkably, the EL can be fully
manipulated with pronounced magnetic hysteresis by spin-flip transitions; Meanwhile, the EL can
be modulated with spin-canting features by perpendicular fields with respect to the easy axis.
Moreover, the modulation of EL efficiency during these two spin transitions shows the opposite
trend, due to the distinct magneto-resistance responses in these two cases.

In this prototype spin-LED, the air-stable vdW CrSBr is selected as the magnetic medium
with layer-dependent magnetism including ferromagnetic (FM), Ferrimagnetic (FiM) and
antiferromagnetic (AFM) phases28-32. This selection is deliberated based on the unique
exciton/electron-spin interactions in CrSBr as elucidated in recent reports28. Due to the 2D
quantum confinements, strong anisotropy and 2D magnetism, CrSBr exhibits unconventional
light-matter interactions for photoluminescence (PL)33, surface and bulk excitons34,35, exciton
polaritons36-38, exciton-phonon/exciton-magnon coupling39,40 and unique exciton dynamics41.
Moreover, CrSBr also supports distinct spin-charge coupling for spin-dependent charge transfer42
and electrostatic control of spin polarization in heterostructures31. This design is rooted in the
insight that carrier injection can dynamically tune interlayer exchange energy and itinerant
ferromagnetic components in CrSBr, enabling EL to serve as a functional readout of magnetic
phase transitions—filling the gap between magnetic characterization and practical opto-spintronic
devices. It is important to distinguish the operational paradigm of such spin-LEDs from
conventional ones. Typical spin-LEDs encode spin information into the circular polarization of
emitted light43,44. The device we demonstrate encodes the magnetic order state—leveraging spin
transitions—into the emission energy, intensity, and its hysteretic memory, while the output light
remains robustly linearly polarized due to the intrinsic anisotropy of material. This establishes a
distinct mechanism of magnetic-order-modulated EL.

During the preparation of this manuscript, we became aware of two related studies reporting
polarized or polaritonic EL in CrSBr via tunneling-based structures68,69. While these works
demonstrate the feasibility of CrSBr-based light emission, our study achieves a spin-LED in which
the EL itself exhibits pronounced magnetic hysteresis linked to spin-flip transitions and can be
continuously tuned via spin canting. Furthermore, we establish efficient operation down to the
bilayer limit and demonstrate dual-mode magnetic control of both spectral and intensity response
within a designed QW architecture. We demonstrate that electrical injection does not merely
replicate PL behavior but unlocks new functionalities—magnetic memory readout, layer-resolved
control, and spintronic-photonic coupling—thereby providing the essential device concept and
operational principles for future integrated opto-spintronics. These features transform the device
into a functional, non-volatile spin-optoelectronic component, representing a critical step toward
integrated magneto-photonic systems.

In addition, recent reports have demonstrated spin-polarized EL in CrI /TMD heterostructures,
3
where TMDs serve as the light-emitting layer and CrI provides spin polarization. Our work differs
3
fundamentally by using CrSBr as both the magnetic medium and light-emitting layer—eliminating
interface spin scattering and simplifying architecture. Unlike CrI , which only supports out-of-
3
plane spin-flip transitions, CrSBr enables dual spin-transition control (in-plane spin-flip and out-
of-plane spin-canting) for EL modulation with hysteretic/continuous behaviors and a higher
efficiency. CrSBr also exhibits superior air stability compared to air-sensitive CrI
3
. Beyond 2D
systems, our device addresses limitations of traditional magnetic LEDs—low efficiency (<30%),
interface disorder, unstable polarization—by leveraging the intrinsic magnetism of CrSBr to
achieve 73.8% modulation efficiency and near-100% stable linear EL polarization. Prior 2D
magnet-based opto-spintronic devices lacked spin-modulated LEDs, and our work fills this gap by
demonstrating the first prototype with a single 2D magnetic semiconductor down to the bilayer
limit, enabled by strong intrinsic magneto-excitonic interactions.

In summary, the prototype spin-LED, as a core scheme of opto-spintronic devices, has been
realized and manifests spin-transitions modulated EL down to bilayers of vdW CrSBr. Unlike
conventional spin-LEDs that output spin information as circular polarization, our device
transduces magnetic order into tunable emission wavelength and intensity with inherent memory,
representing a magnetic-order-modulated LED paradigm. Particularly, the EL hysteresis
demonstrates that carrier injection can actively engineer interlayer exchange energy in 2D CrSBr.
Besides the spin-order dressed excitonic transitions for the EL spectral resonances, the EL
efficiency is directly determined by the spintronic transport, which shows opposite magnetic-
modulated trends for spin-flip and spin-canting transitions. This study establishes the prototype
device architecture for spin-LED, which essentially merges photonic, electronic, and magnetic
functionalities. Moreover, it also promises many opportunities to develop magnetic sensors,
magnetic tunneling junctions, integrated 2D opto-spintronic chip for neuromorphic computing.
paper_content.methods:
Synthesis of CrSBr.
CrSBr single crystals were synthesized via chemical vapor transport (CVT, Wuhan Shiwei
Optoelectronic Technology Co., Ltd.). Chromium (III) bromide (CrBr , 99.00% purity, Macklin),
3
sulfur powder (S, 99.95% purity, Aladdin), and Chromium powder (Cr, 99.00% purity, thermo
scientific) were used as precursors. A stoichiometric mixture of CrBr (720 g), S (196 g), and Cr
3
(189 g) was sealed within an evacuated quartz ampoule using an oil-free molecular pump under a
high vacuum. The ampoule was subjected to a controlled thermal gradient. The source zone
temperature was programmed as follows: ramped to 500 °C over 6 h, then to 550 °C over 12 h,
subsequently to 930 °C over 12 h, and finally held at 930 °C for 84 h before cooling naturally to
room temperature. Concurrently, the growth zone temperature profile was: ramped to 570 °C over
6 h and held for 12 h, then increased to 970 °C over 12 h and maintained for 24 h, followed by
cooling to 850 °C over 12 h and holding for 48 h, before natural cooling to room temperature. The
resulting crystals were recovered and stored within an argon-filled glove box upon opening the
ampoule.

Thin flakes of CrSBr were prepared using the scotch magic tape-based mechanical exfoliation
technique. Prior to exfoliation, SiO /Si substrates were treated with oxygen plasma for 10 min to
2
remove surface adsorbates and enhance adhesion. CrSBr crystals were then mechanically
exfoliated directly onto the treated SiO /Si substrates. All exfoliation procedures were performed
2
under ambient conditions at room temperature.

Sample fabrication
QW devices were fabricated using graphite, hBN, and exfoliated CrSBr flakes. Graphite and
hBN crystals were sourced from HQ Graphene. Flake thickness selection for graphite and hBN
followed the criteria established in our previous work70. Both materials were mechanically
exfoliated onto SiO /Si substrates. Dark-field optical microscopy confirmed the flakes possessed
2
clean surfaces and uniform quality, qualifying them for quantum well assembly. CrSBr flakes of
varying layer numbers were initially identified via optical microscopy contrast and subsequently
had their thickness verified by atomic force microscopy. Device assembly was performed on a
transfer stage. A polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)/polycarbonate (PC) stamp was used to
sequentially pick up the constituent layers (graphite, hBN, CrSBr, hBN, graphite) at 80 °C. The
assembled stack was then transferred onto pre-patterned electrodes. These electrodes were
fabricated by ultraviolet photolithography followed by thermal evaporation of a 5 nm chromium
adhesion layer and a 50 nm gold layer. During the transfer, the PC film was melted onto the
electrode structure. Finally, the completed device was immersed in chloroform to dissolve residual
PC. This was followed by sequential 5-minute immersions in acetone and isopropanol to ensure
the surface remained clean and free of contaminants.

Experimental setup
The experimental setup for PL, EL, and electrical characterization incorporated a closed-loop
cryofree magneto-optical system (attoLDRY 2100) featuring a 9 T superconducting magnet (out-
of-plane) and an attocube piezo-driven xyz translation stage. Optical spectra (PL and EL) were
collected using a WITec Alpha 300R confocal microscope. PL was excited with a 532 nm laser
focused to a spot size of approximately 1 micrometer. Device voltage control was managed by a
Keysight B1500A parameter analyzer. AFM imaging in contact mode was conducted on a Bruker
DIMENSION ICON instrument employing a DDESP-V2 cantilever (force constant: 80 N/m,
resonance frequency: 450 kHz).

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available in the main text and Supplementary
Information. Additional data may be obtained from the corresponding author upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have made a clear effort to address my previous comments and have added additional experiments and analyses to strengthen their claims. The revision helps clarify several aspects of the device behavior and supports the central conclusions of the manuscript. Nevertheless, some points related to the physical interpretation—particularly concerning the relationship between hysteresis, energy dissipation, and transport-related metrics—would benefit from further clarification. The corresponding suggestions are listed below. After the authors address these issues through a major revision, I believe the work would be much improved and suitable for publication.
1. Continuing the previous comment 1. While the authors provide several arguments supporting a predominantly magnetic origin of the EL modulation, the current evidence does not fully exclude thickness-dependent injection effects. In particular, although the h-BN layers are designed to act as uniform tunneling barriers, the effective carrier injection into CrSBr may still depend on the electronic structure of the CrSBr layer itself, which is known to evolve with thickness. To further rule out residual injection-related effects (e.g., thickness-dependent effective barriers), the authors are encouraged to provide voltage-dependent EL intensity measurements for devices with different CrSBr thicknesses. A comparison of the EL turn-on behavior (similar to Fig. 1e and Fig. S6) across different layer numbers would serve as a direct control experiment to demonstrate that carrier injection is largely independent of CrSBr thickness, thereby strengthening the conclusion that the observed EL modulation is purely magnetic in origin.
2. Continuing the previous comment 4. The hysteresis loop area reflects the energy dissipation associated with changes in spin configuration, including spin-flip transitions. The processes are intrinsic to the magnetic spin ordering of the CrSBr layers. In this context, current density and EQE are not the natural parameters governing spin-configuration-related dissipation. Varying the current density at a fixed thickness primarily probes carrier injection and transport, but does not modify the underlying spin configuration responsible for the hysteresis. Therefore, the observation that the hysteresis loop area remains unchanged with current density while EQE decreases does not directly support the conclusion that hysteresis-related dissipation is decoupled from EL efficiency in general. A discussion focusing on thickness-dependent hysteresis would be more physically relevant than a current-density-dependent analysis, since the spin ordering in CrSBr evolves with layer number.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have satisfactorily addressed all of my concerns in the revision. I therefore recommend publication in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overall, I find that my specific technical questions have been addressed satisfactorily, and I appreciate the additional data and clarifications provided in the revised manuscript. That said, I want to emphasize that several points raised by other reviewers appear more central to the paper’s impact.
One remaining issue for me concerns the interpretation of the electroluminescence hysteresis. While the authors demonstrate convincingly that EL hysteresis is more pronounced than PL hysteresis, the physical origin and broader significance of this difference remain insufficiently explained. In particular, it is still unclear why EL hysteresis is fundamentally distinct from PL hysteresis, rather than simply a manifestation of transport-modulated intensity, and what new insight this provides into spin–exciton coupling or magnetic phase transitions in CrSBr. I encourage the authors to articulate more clearly what is qualitatively new about EL hysteresis compared to PL, beyond the presence of carrier injection.
Finally, I note that several parts of the rebuttal, including the response to my Q1 and the responses to Reviewer 4 Q1 and Q2, read as highly templated and generic. This makes it difficult to judge whether the authors have fully engaged with the underlying physical concerns, as opposed to providing broadly applicable rebuttal language. A more mechanism-driven discussion that directly addresses the conceptual implications would substantially strengthen the manuscript.

(Remarks to the Author)

voltages are all ~2.5 V across devices with 3-layer (2.5 V) to 15-layer (2 V) CrSBr—exhibiting

independent of CrSBr thickness.
Figure S6. Voltage-dependent EL intensity of 3-layer (red), 9-layer (yellow) and 15-
layer (light blue) CrSBr QW device at 2 K.

the CrSBr layer itself. Collectively, these supplementary experiments effectively rule

strongly reinforce our conclusion that the observed EL modulation originates from

(Remarks to the Author)
Overall, I find that my specific technical questions have been addressed satisfactorily,

That said, I want to emphasize that several points raised by other reviewers appear more

One remaining issue for me concerns the interpretation of the electroluminescence
hysteresis. While the authors demonstrate convincingly that EL hysteresis is more
pronounced than PL hysteresis, the physical origin and broader significance of this
difference remain insufficiently explained. In particular, it is still unclear why EL
hysteresis is fundamentally distinct from PL hysteresis, rather than simply a

Response：
Thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the physical origin of the
enhanced EL hysteresis. We clarify that the fundamental distinction lies in the active
role of injected carriers. For PL, the optical excitation generates excitons that act
primarily as passive probes of the existing magnetic order. In contrast, EL involves the
continuous injection of spin-polarized electrons and holes through the CrSBr layers.
These injected carriers do not merely "light up" the material; they actively modulate
interlayer exchange interaction⁠1,2⁠.
The carrier-mediated modulation of magnetic interactions has been well-
established in 2D vdW magnets: CrI exhibits electric field-tuned FM-AFM balance
3
and gate-induced magnetic phase transitions1,3; Cr Ge Te shows gating-modulated
2 2 6
magnetization loops via Fermi level shifts⁠4; CrSBr itself has electrostatic doping-tuned
interlayer exchange energy and enhanced hysteresis5. These precedents confirm that
carrier doping/injection is a generic pathway to actively manipulate magnetic
interactions in vdW magnets.
This active modulation of interlayer coupling by carrier injection represents a
qualitatively new insight into the magnetic phase transitions of CrSBr. Consistent with
our thickness-dependent observations (Figure S10)—where stronger intrinsic interlayer
coupling correlated with larger EL hysteresis—we attribute the enhanced hysteresis to
carrier-mediated stabilization of the magnetic order.⁠ While the precise microscopic
dynamics of these spin-carrier interactions remain a rich area for future inquiry, the
current data explicitly distinguishes the active nature of EL from the passive readout of
PL.
To ensure these fundamental distinction and qualitatively new insight are clearly
articulated throughout the revised manuscript, we added targeted statements as shown
in our response to Comment-2

makes it difficult to judge whether the authors have fully engaged with the underlying
physical concerns, as opposed to providing broadly applicable rebuttal language. A
more mechanism-driven discussion that directly addresses the conceptual
implications would substantially strengthen the manuscript.

We take this critique very seriously. We apologize if our previous responses
appeared generic; our intent was to provide a concise overview, but we recognize this
may have obscured the specific physical insights driving our work. In this revision, we
have moved beyond broad descriptions to provide a strictly mechanism-driven
discussion, particularly linking the device performance to the microscopic spin-charge
interactions in CrSBr.
Our selection of CrSBr as the core system is rooted in its unique intrinsic
properties that enable CrSBr to serve as both a magnetic medium and a light-
emitting layer, eliminating the need for additional functional layers. This
mechanism-driven design is what fundamentally distinguishes our work from prior
studies6-10. Our QW structure enables active carrier-mediated modulation of
interlayer AFM coupling—amplifying the energy barrier for AFM-FM transitions and
leading to more prominent EL hysteresis than PL. Its orthorhombic crystal symmetry
further endows biaxial magnetic anisotropy, supporting dual spin-transition pathways:
in-plane spin-flip (B//b) triggers an AFM-to-FM phase transition with non-volatile
EL hysteresis, while out-of-plane spin-canting (B//c) enables continuous EL
tuning—functionalities unattainable in CrI or conventional systems11-13. This
3
integration eliminates interface losses and defect-induced non-radiative recombination,
achieving a record-high modulation efficiency of 73.8%, near-unity field-insensitive
linear polarization, and air stability, thus addressing the long-standing limitations of
low efficiency, poor stability, and single-mode control in prior magnetic LEDs12,14,15.
To ensure these mechanism-driven innovations are clearly articulated throughout

Abstract (page 2, line 10):
Notably, the intrinsic carrier-tunable interlayer magnetic coupling in CrSBr enables

This design is rooted in the insight that carrier injection can dynamically tune

EL to serve as a functional readout of magnetic phase transitions—filling the gap

It is also noted that the EL hysteresis is more prominent than that of PL. This might be

Unlike conventional spin-LEDs that output spin information as circular polarization,
our device transduces magnetic order into tunable emission wavelength and intensity
with inherent memory, representing a magnetic-order-modulated LED paradigm.
Particularly, the EL hysteresis demonstrates that carrier injection can actively engineer
interlayer exchange energy in 2D CrSBr.
These additions, combined with our focus on mechanism-driven design emphasize
that our innovation stems from intrinsic physical interactions rather than external
modifications. By intentionally designing a structure to leverage carrier-tunable
magnetic propertiesn in CrSBr, we realized a spin-LED with non-volatile hysteretic
control, continuous analog modulation, and spintronic-photonic integration—

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Emerging two-dimensional magnetic semiconductors represent transformative platforms to
explore magneto-optics and opto-spintronic applications. Though two-dimensional opto-
spintronics has attracted tremendous research efforts in spin-dependent photodetectors and non-
volatile memory components, the realization of one core application - spin-modulated light-
emitting device - remains elusive so far. Here we successfully realize prototype spin-modulated
light-emitting device integrated with a two-dimensional semiconducting magnet chromium sulfide
bromide, demonstrating considerable electroluminescence down to bilayers. Intriguingly, its
discovered to be directly manipulated by spin-flip and spin-canting transitions. Notably, the
intrinsic carrier-tunable interlayer magnetic coupling in chromium sulfide bromide enables
electroluminescence to actively amplify magnetic hysteresis (via spin-flip) and continuously tune
magnetic order (via spin-canting) with robust anisotropy, establishing a connection between carrier
injection, magnetic phase transitions, and optical emission. The prototype demonstration of spin-
modulated light-emitting device establishes an indispensable scheme of opto-spintronic devices
leveraging two-dimensional spin transitions and strong excitonic effects, presenting a critical step
towards integrated two-dimensional opto-spintronics.

---

## Introduction

Opto-spintronics, merging photonic, electronic, and magnetic functionalities, becomes a
novel but desirable paradigm for future information technologies1-4. Compared with conventional
charge-based electronics, this paradigm exploits electron spins as the fundamental variable for
information processing and storage, promising new functionalities with significantly reduced
energy consumption. For instance, non-volatile memory devices feature optical writing and
electrical readout of the spin orders5,6, and neuromorphic computing hardware employ spin-based
artificial synapses7. By leveraging spin-wave excitations, opto-magnonic circuits and quantum
transduction platforms have also been proposed and developed8. As one of the fundamental
optoelectronic components, light-emitting devices (LEDs) advance to unexplored versatility when
their electrical injections involve profound spin manipulations9-12. A critical bottleneck in opto-
spintronics is cryogenic operation (<10 K) of spin-dependent effects, far from practical room-
temperature requirements. This stems from the thermal fragility of two-dimensional (2D) magnetic
order and enhanced non-radiative recombination in 2D semiconductors.

The emerging vdW magnets have been recently extensively studied for striking fundamental
physical breakthroughs with unconventional 2D magnetism13,14. The confluence of inherent 2D
magnetism, electronic structures, and weak dielectric screening in the layered structures suggests
unprecedented functionalities to opto-spintronic components9. For example, spin-dependent
photodetectors15-17, spin-photovoltaics18 with magnetic CrI and MnSe have been proposed;
3
Moreover, non-volatile memory component with magnetic four-layer CrI and VSe has also been
3 2
designed19. However, as one core application of 2D opto-spintronics, no LED with spin-based
functionality has been realized so far20-23. Here, we report the realization of a prototype spin-
modulated LED (spin-LED) in CrSBr-based quantum well (QW) structures, achieving
considerable electroluminescence (EL) down to bilayer CrSBr. Unlike EL in conventional
semiconductors dictated by band structure and carrier recombinations24-27, the spin-exciton
coupling in CrSBr introduces versatile manipulations of its EL. Remarkably, the EL can be fully
manipulated with pronounced magnetic hysteresis by spin-flip transitions; Meanwhile, the EL can
be modulated with spin-canting features by perpendicular fields with respect to the easy axis.
Moreover, the modulation of EL efficiency during these two spin transitions shows the opposite
trend, due to the distinct magneto-resistance responses in these two cases.

In this prototype spin-LED, the air-stable vdW CrSBr is selected as the magnetic medium
with layer-dependent magnetism including ferromagnetic (FM), Ferrimagnetic (FiM) and
antiferromagnetic (AFM) phases28-32. This selection is deliberated based on the unique
exciton/electron-spin interactions in CrSBr as elucidated in recent reports28. Due to the 2D
quantum confinements, strong anisotropy and 2D magnetism, CrSBr exhibits unconventional
light-matter interactions for photoluminescence (PL)33, surface and bulk excitons34,35, exciton
polaritons36-38, exciton-phonon/exciton-magnon coupling39,40 and unique exciton dynamics41.
Moreover, CrSBr also supports distinct spin-charge coupling for spin-dependent charge transfer42
and electrostatic control of spin polarization in heterostructures31. This design is rooted in the
insight that carrier injection can dynamically tune interlayer exchange energy and itinerant
ferromagnetic components in CrSBr, enabling EL to serve as a functional readout of magnetic
phase transitions—filling the gap between magnetic characterization and practical opto-spintronic
devices. It is important to distinguish the operational paradigm of such spin-LEDs from
conventional ones. Typical spin-LEDs encode spin information into the circular polarization of
emitted light43,44. The device we demonstrate encodes the magnetic order state—leveraging spin
transitions—into the emission energy, intensity, and its hysteretic memory, while the output light
remains robustly linearly polarized due to the intrinsic anisotropy of material. This establishes a
distinct mechanism of magnetic-order-modulated EL.

---

## Results

EL characterization in CrSBr

Sample configuration and characterizations. To probe the intrinsic EL properties of CrSBr,
a tunneling LED integrated with a QW structure is designed and fabricated (see Supplementary
Section 1 Fig. S1, S2 for sample preparations). The QW structure consists of a few-layer CrSBr
flake sandwiched between top and bottom graphite (G) electrodes, with upper and lower barrier
layers of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) (Fig. 1a). In this device design, electrons and holes are
injected into the CrSBr flake by tunneling through hBN from top and bottom G, respectively (Fig.
1b). This design is crucial as it provides clean interfaces and minimizes defect-induced scattering,
both essential for achieving high-quality optical and electrical performance45-47. As a result, few-
layer CrSBr samples not only show clear PL spectra of bulk (X ) and surface (X ) excitons, but
b s
also more importantly exhibit unambiguous EL spectra as well. Fig. 1c shows the CrSBr thickness-
dependent spectral features of X and X in the device structure, which are consistent with the
b s
previously reported excitonic emissions in CrSBr34. Specifically, the PL features only one peak of
X ~ 1.34 eV (the blue segment) in the bilayer (2L) CrSBr, and starts to embrace another peak of
s

b
(Supplementary Section 1 Fig. S3). As the CrSBr thickness increases to 15 layers (15L), the PL
spectrum is dominated by the peak of X . Note here two split peaks of X in the 15L sample may
b s
be due to two X experiencing slightly different dielectric environments34,35. Expectedly, this
s
thickness dependence originates from the layered structure and the AFM orders of CrSBr, making
X

dielectric environments34.

Observation of EL. With the PL characterizations in these CrSBr LED samples, the EL has
been successfully observed with prominent thickness dependence (Fig. 1d). Apparently, all the EL
spectra are dominated by X , where its peaks are consistent with the PL spectra, but their full-

N

EL

Moreover, similar EL linear polarization is also observed in 9-layer CrSBr device (see

3

3

high vacuum. The ampoule was subjected to a controlled thermal gradient. The source zone
temperature was programmed as follows: ramped to 500 °C over 6 h, then to 550 °C over 12 h,
subsequently to 930 °C over 12 h, and finally held at 930 °C for 84 h before cooling naturally to
room temperature. Concurrently, the growth zone temperature profile was: ramped to 570 °C over
6 h and held for 12 h, then increased to 970 °C over 12 h and maintained for 24 h, followed by
cooling to 850 °C over 12 h and holding for 48 h, before natural cooling to room temperature. The
resulting crystals were recovered and stored within an argon-filled glove box upon opening the
ampoule.

Thin flakes of CrSBr were prepared using the scotch magic tape-based mechanical exfoliation
technique. Prior to exfoliation, SiO /Si substrates were treated with oxygen plasma for 10 min to
2
remove surface adsorbates and enhance adhesion. CrSBr crystals were then mechanically
exfoliated directly onto the treated SiO /Si substrates. All exfoliation procedures were performed
2

exfoliated onto SiO /Si substrates. Dark-field optical microscopy confirmed the flakes possessed
2

transfer stage. A polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)/polycarbonate (PC) stamp was used to
sequentially pick up the constituent layers (graphite, hBN, CrSBr, hBN, graphite) at 80 °C. The
assembled stack was then transferred onto pre-patterned electrodes. These electrodes were
fabricated by ultraviolet photolithography followed by thermal evaporation of a 5 nm chromium
adhesion layer and a 50 nm gold layer. During the transfer, the PC film was melted onto the
electrode structure. Finally, the completed device was immersed in chloroform to dissolve residual
PC. This was followed by sequential 5-minute immersions in acetone and isopropanol to ensure
the surface remained clean and free of contaminants.

The experimental setup for PL, EL, and electrical characterization incorporated a closed-loop
cryofree magneto-optical system (attoLDRY 2100) featuring a 9 T superconducting magnet (out-

## Introduction

Opto-spintronics, merging photonic, electronic, and magnetic functionalities, becomes a
novel but desirable paradigm for future information technologies1-4. Compared with conventional
charge-based electronics, this paradigm exploits electron spins as the fundamental variable for
information processing and storage, promising new functionalities with significantly reduced
energy consumption. For instance, non-volatile memory devices feature optical writing and
electrical readout of the spin orders5,6, and neuromorphic computing hardware employ spin-based
artificial synapses7. By leveraging spin-wave excitations, opto-magnonic circuits and quantum
transduction platforms have also been proposed and developed8. As one of the fundamental
optoelectronic components, light-emitting devices (LEDs) advance to unexplored versatility when
their electrical injections involve profound spin manipulations9-12. A critical bottleneck in opto-
spintronics is cryogenic operation (<10 K) of spin-dependent effects, far from practical room-
temperature requirements. This stems from the thermal fragility of two-dimensional (2D) magnetic
order and enhanced non-radiative recombination in 2D semiconductors.

The emerging vdW magnets have been recently extensively studied for striking fundamental
physical breakthroughs with unconventional 2D magnetism13,14. The confluence of inherent 2D
magnetism, electronic structures, and weak dielectric screening in the layered structures suggests
unprecedented functionalities to opto-spintronic components9. For example, spin-dependent
photodetectors15-17, spin-photovoltaics18 with magnetic CrI and MnSe have been proposed;

3 2

functionality has been realized so far20-23. Here, we report the realization of a prototype spin-
modulated LED (spin-LED) in CrSBr-based quantum well (QW) structures, achieving
considerable electroluminescence (EL) down to bilayer CrSBr. Unlike EL in conventional
semiconductors dictated by band structure and carrier recombinations24-27, the spin-exciton
coupling in CrSBr introduces versatile manipulations of its EL. Remarkably, the EL can be fully
manipulated with pronounced magnetic hysteresis by spin-flip transitions; Meanwhile, the EL can
be modulated with spin-canting features by perpendicular fields with respect to the easy axis.
Moreover, the modulation of EL efficiency during these two spin transitions shows the opposite
trend, due to the distinct magneto-resistance responses in these two cases.

with layer-dependent magnetism including ferromagnetic (FM), Ferrimagnetic (FiM) and
antiferromagnetic (AFM) phases28-32. This selection is deliberated based on the unique
exciton/electron-spin interactions in CrSBr as elucidated in recent reports28. Due to the 2D

light-matter interactions for photoluminescence (PL)33, surface and bulk excitons34,35, exciton

## Methods

Synthesis of CrSBr.
CrSBr single crystals were synthesized via chemical vapor transport (CVT, Wuhan Shiwei
Optoelectronic Technology Co., Ltd.). Chromium (III) bromide (CrBr , 99.00% purity, Macklin),
3
sulfur powder (S, 99.95% purity, Aladdin), and Chromium powder (Cr, 99.00% purity, thermo
scientific) were used as precursors. A stoichiometric mixture of CrBr (720 g), S (196 g), and Cr
3
(189 g) was sealed within an evacuated quartz ampoule using an oil-free molecular pump under a
high vacuum. The ampoule was subjected to a controlled thermal gradient. The source zone
temperature was programmed as follows: ramped to 500 °C over 6 h, then to 550 °C over 12 h,
subsequently to 930 °C over 12 h, and finally held at 930 °C for 84 h before cooling naturally to
room temperature. Concurrently, the growth zone temperature profile was: ramped to 570 °C over
6 h and held for 12 h, then increased to 970 °C over 12 h and maintained for 24 h, followed by
cooling to 850 °C over 12 h and holding for 48 h, before natural cooling to room temperature. The
resulting crystals were recovered and stored within an argon-filled glove box upon opening the
ampoule.

Thin flakes of CrSBr were prepared using the scotch magic tape-based mechanical exfoliation
technique. Prior to exfoliation, SiO /Si substrates were treated with oxygen plasma for 10 min to
2
remove surface adsorbates and enhance adhesion. CrSBr crystals were then mechanically
exfoliated directly onto the treated SiO /Si substrates. All exfoliation procedures were performed
2
under ambient conditions at room temperature.

Sample fabrication
QW devices were fabricated using graphite, hBN, and exfoliated CrSBr flakes. Graphite and
hBN crystals were sourced from HQ Graphene. Flake thickness selection for graphite and hBN
followed the criteria established in our previous work70. Both materials were mechanically
exfoliated onto SiO /Si substrates. Dark-field optical microscopy confirmed the flakes possessed
2
clean surfaces and uniform quality, qualifying them for quantum well assembly. CrSBr flakes of
varying layer numbers were initially identified via optical microscopy contrast and subsequently
had their thickness verified by atomic force microscopy. Device assembly was performed on a
transfer stage. A polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)/polycarbonate (PC) stamp was used to
sequentially pick up the constituent layers (graphite, hBN, CrSBr, hBN, graphite) at 80 °C. The
assembled stack was then transferred onto pre-patterned electrodes. These electrodes were
fabricated by ultraviolet photolithography followed by thermal evaporation of a 5 nm chromium
adhesion layer and a 50 nm gold layer. During the transfer, the PC film was melted onto the
electrode structure. Finally, the completed device was immersed in chloroform to dissolve residual
PC. This was followed by sequential 5-minute immersions in acetone and isopropanol to ensure
the surface remained clean and free of contaminants.

Experimental setup
The experimental setup for PL, EL, and electrical characterization incorporated a closed-loop
cryofree magneto-optical system (attoLDRY 2100) featuring a 9 T superconducting magnet (out-
of-plane) and an attocube piezo-driven xyz translation stage. Optical spectra (PL and EL) were
collected using a WITec Alpha 300R confocal microscope. PL was excited with a 532 nm laser
focused to a spot size of approximately 1 micrometer. Device voltage control was managed by a
Keysight B1500A parameter analyzer. AFM imaging in contact mode was conducted on a Bruker
DIMENSION ICON instrument employing a DDESP-V2 cantilever (force constant: 80 N/m,
resonance frequency: 450 kHz).

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available in the main text and Supplementary
Information. Additional data may be obtained from the corresponding author upon request.

In particular, although the h-BN layers are designed to act as uniform tunneling barriers, the effective carrier injection into CrSBr may still depend on the electronic structure of the CrSBr layer itself, which is known to evolve with thickness. The processes are intrinsic to the magnetic spin ordering of the CrSBr layers. Varying the current density at a fixed thickness primarily probes carrier injection and transport, but does not modify the underlying spin configuration responsible for the hysteresis. A discussion focusing on thickness-dependent hysteresis would be more physically relevant than a current-density-dependent analysis, since the spin ordering in CrSBr evolves with layer number.

temperature was programmed as follows: ramped to 500 °C over 6 h, then to 550 °C over 12 h,
subsequently to 930 °C over 12 h, and finally held at 930 °C for 84 h before cooling naturally to
room temperature. Concurrently, the growth zone temperature profile was: ramped to 570 °C over
6 h and held for 12 h, then increased to 970 °C over 12 h and maintained for 24 h, followed by

Thin flakes of CrSBr were prepared using the scotch magic tape-based mechanical exfoliation
technique. Prior to exfoliation, SiO /Si substrates were treated with oxygen plasma for 10 min to
2
remove surface adsorbates and enhance adhesion. CrSBr crystals were then mechanically

2
